body:
Meaning of foreign policy

Foreign policy refers to the principles, objectives and decisions through which a country conducts its relations with other countries and international organisations. It covers matters such as national security, diplomatic relations, international trade, treaties, peace and cooperation.

India became independent on 15 August 1947. Political independence gave the country the authority to make its own decisions in international affairs. However, independence also created the responsibility to protect national security and establish relations with other countries.

India's early foreign policy was shaped by Jawaharlal Nehru, who served as both the first Prime Minister and the External Affairs Minister. He exercised a major influence over foreign-policy decisions during the period from 1946 to 1964.

The international situation after 1945

The Second World War ended in 1945. Much of Europe had suffered extensive destruction, and 2 countries emerged as the principal superpowers: the United States of America (USA) and the Union of Soviet Socialist Republics (USSR).

Their rivalry developed into the Cold War. This was a period of political, ideological and military competition without a full-scale direct war between the 2 superpowers. The USA generally supported capitalism and liberal democracy, while the USSR promoted a communist political and economic system.

The Cold War divided much of the world into rival groups. The US-led North Atlantic Treaty Organization (NATO) was established in 1949, while the Soviet-led Warsaw Pact was formed in 1955.

Newly independent countries faced pressure to associate with one of these powerful groups. India needed international assistance for development but did not want such assistance to determine its political independence.

India's circumstances in 1947

Several domestic and international factors influenced India's foreign policy:

  • Recent colonial experience: India valued sovereignty because it had only recently secured independence from British rule.
  • Partition and security: Partition created tensions with Pakistan, including the dispute over Jammu and Kashmir.
  • Economic difficulties: Poverty, limited industrial development and shortages of resources made economic progress an urgent priority.
  • Decolonisation: Many Asian and African countries were struggling for independence. India supported their freedom from colonial rule.
  • Cold War rivalry: India sought to avoid becoming dependent on either superpower.

Major objectives of Nehru's foreign policy

India's early foreign policy had 3 principal objectives:

  1. Preserving sovereignty: India should remain politically independent and make its own international decisions.
  2. Protecting territorial integrity: India should defend its territory and national security against external threats.
  3. Promoting economic development: Peaceful international conditions should allow India to concentrate on industrialisation, poverty reduction and national development.

These objectives were closely related. Maintaining peace could reduce the diversion of scarce resources towards warfare. Independent decision-making could also help India obtain economic and technical assistance from different countries without becoming subordinate to one superpower.

Constitutional basis: Article 51

Article 51 of the Constitution of India forms part of the Directive Principles of State Policy. It directs the State to endeavour to:

  • Promote international peace and security.
  • Maintain just and honourable relations between nations.
  • Foster respect for international law and treaty obligations.
  • Encourage settlement of international disputes by arbitration.

Arbitration means referring a dispute to an agreed third party or tribunal for a decision instead of resolving it through force.

As a Directive Principle, Article 51 guides government policy but is not directly enforceable by courts in the same manner as Fundamental Rights. It expresses constitutional objectives rather than prohibiting India from defending itself against aggression.

India therefore sought peaceful international relations while retaining the right to protect its national interests.

Prelims focus

  • India became independent on 15 August 1947.
  • The Cold War was principally a rivalry between the USA and USSR.
  • NATO was established in 1949; the Warsaw Pact was formed in 1955.
  • Jawaharlal Nehru was India's first Prime Minister and also served as External Affairs Minister.
  • Article 51 concerns the promotion of international peace and security.
  • Trap: Article 51 is a Directive Principle, not a Fundamental Right.

[Sources: NCERT, Politics in India since Independence, Class 12, chapter 4, India's External Relations, printed pp. 65-67; NCERT, Contemporary World Politics, Class 12, chapter 1, The Cold War Era, printed pp. 3-6; Constitution of India, Article 51, Legislative Department edition as at 11 November 2025, consulted 22 November 2026.]

pictures.caption: Independent India began making its own foreign-policy decisions in a world divided by the Cold War.

pictures.alt: India, independent in 1947, joined neither NATO nor the Warsaw Pact and pursued non-alignment to protect sovereignty, territory and development.

title: India's Foreign Policy After Independence: Background, Objectives and Principles

body:
What is strategic autonomy?

Strategic autonomy is the ability of a country to make important foreign-policy and security decisions according to its own national interests, without allowing another country or military bloc to dictate those decisions.

Strategic autonomy does not require a country to avoid international cooperation. A strategically autonomous country may purchase equipment, receive economic assistance, enter into agreements or cooperate with other countries while retaining the freedom to decide its position on each issue.

For independent India, strategic autonomy was especially important because British colonial rule had deprived Indians of control over their country's external relations.

Meaning of non-alignment

Non-alignment was India's principal strategy for preserving independent foreign-policy choices during the Cold War.

It meant remaining outside the rival military alliances led by the USA and the USSR. India did not accept that every international dispute required it to support one superpower against the other.

Instead, India sought to examine international issues according to their merits, national interests and principles such as peaceful coexistence and opposition to colonialism.

This allowed India to maintain relations with both superpowers and obtain assistance from countries belonging to different political systems.

Non-alignment is not neutrality or isolationism

Three concepts must be distinguished carefully.

Non-alignment

A non-aligned country avoids joining rival military blocs but can participate actively in international affairs. It may support diplomatic negotiations, criticise aggression, assist peace efforts or defend itself if attacked.

Neutrality

Neutrality generally refers to a country's position of not participating as a belligerent in a particular war. Legal neutrality during an international armed conflict carries duties regarding the treatment of the belligerents.

A neutral country may also undertake diplomatic or humanitarian activities, but its neutrality is primarily concerned with its conduct during war.

Isolationism

Isolationism refers to a policy of substantially limiting involvement in international political or military affairs. India did not adopt isolationism because it actively participated in international organisations, supported decolonisation and sought to reduce international tensions.

Non-alignment does not mean remaining equally distant from every country on every issue. It means retaining independent judgment instead of accepting a permanent obligation to follow one rival power bloc.

How India practised non-alignment

Cooperation with both superpowers

India sought diplomatic, economic and technical cooperation from countries belonging to both Cold War blocs. Such cooperation could support national development without requiring India to become a member of either bloc.

Participation in international peace efforts

India supported the United Nations and participated in international peacekeeping and diplomatic efforts. During the Korean War in the early 1950s, Indian representatives contributed to diplomatic efforts aimed at reducing tensions.

Opposition to colonialism and racial discrimination

India supported independence movements in Asia and Africa and opposed apartheid, the system of institutionalised racial segregation and discrimination in South Africa.

Independent positions on international crises

India opposed the British-French-Israeli military intervention in Egypt during the Suez Crisis of 1956. However, it did not join the public condemnation of the Soviet intervention in Hungary in the same year.

This difference generated criticism that India's non-alignment was inconsistently applied. It illustrates the distinction between a declared foreign-policy principle and the way governments implement that principle in particular circumstances.

Why non-alignment served India's interests

Non-alignment helped India preserve flexibility. It reduced the pressure to commit itself permanently to one military alliance and enabled the country to seek cooperation from multiple partners.

It also gave India an opportunity to join other newly independent countries in demanding a more representative international order.

However, non-alignment could not eliminate security threats. India still experienced serious conflicts with neighbouring countries. Thus, it was a strategy for independent international decision-making, not a guarantee that war would never occur.

Prelims focus

  • Strategic autonomy means independent decision-making in national interests.
  • Non-alignment meant avoiding membership of rival Cold War military blocs.
  • Non-alignment did not prohibit cooperation with the USA or USSR.
  • India supported diplomatic efforts during the Korean War.
  • India opposed the Suez intervention in 1956.
  • Trap: Non-alignment, neutrality and isolationism are not interchangeable terms.

[Sources: NCERT, Contemporary World Politics, Class 12, chapter 1, The Cold War Era, printed pp. 10-13; NCERT, Politics in India since Independence, Class 12, chapter 4, India's External Relations, printed pp. 66-68.]

pictures.alt: Non-alignment concerns blocs, neutrality concerns a war, and isolationism concerns wider involvement; both non-aligned and neutral states may pursue diplomacy.
pictures.caption: Non-alignment concerns independent foreign-policy choices; neutrality and isolationism address different questions.

title: Strategic Autonomy and Non-Alignment: Meaning, Differences and Practice

body:
Origin and meaning

Panchsheel refers to the Five Principles of Peaceful Coexistence adopted as guiding principles for relations between countries.

They were formally expressed in the preamble to the Agreement on Trade and Intercourse between the Tibet Region of China and India, signed on 29 April 1954.

Jawaharlal Nehru and Chinese Premier Zhou Enlai subsequently promoted these principles as a basis for peaceful relations between countries. Their joint statement of 28 June 1954 extended the significance of Panchsheel beyond relations between India and China.

The principles reflected the belief that countries with different political systems could maintain peaceful relations if they respected one another's independence and legitimate interests.

The 5 principles

  1. Mutual respect for territorial integrity and sovereignty: Each country should respect the other's independence and territory.
  2. Mutual non-aggression: Countries should refrain from aggression against one another.
  3. Mutual non-interference: Countries should not interfere in each other's internal affairs.
  4. Equality and mutual benefit: Countries should deal with one another on the basis of equality and seek benefits through cooperation.
  5. Peaceful coexistence: Countries should maintain peaceful relations despite differences in their political or economic systems.

Understanding the distinctions

Sovereignty and territorial integrity

Sovereignty means the authority of a state to govern itself independently. Territorial integrity means respect for the unity of its territory and the prohibition of unlawful attempts to seize or divide that territory.

Non-aggression and non-interference

Non-aggression concerns hostile actions against another state, particularly the unlawful use of force. Non-interference concerns improper intervention in another state's internal political affairs.

These ideas are related but are not identical. Military aggression may violate both principles, while interference can also occur without an armed attack.

Equality and mutual benefit

This principle rejects the assumption that a powerful country is inherently entitled to dominate a weaker country. It encourages cooperation that recognises the interests of both parties.

Relationship with non-alignment

Panchsheel and non-alignment supported India's broader objective of independent and peaceful foreign relations, but they addressed different matters.

  • Panchsheel describes principles for the conduct of relations between countries.
  • Non-alignment describes the choice to remain outside rival superpower-led military blocs.

A country can support peaceful coexistence while belonging to an alliance. Similarly, a non-aligned country is expected to respect international law but may still become involved in an armed conflict.

Panchsheel, Tibet and the 1962 conflict

The 1954 agreement concerned trade and intercourse between India and the Tibet region of China. It formed part of India's developing diplomatic relations with the People's Republic of China.

However, relations deteriorated as disputes emerged over Tibet and the India-China boundary. The conflict eventually led to the India-China War of 1962.

The war demonstrated that agreement on principles did not necessarily resolve disagreements about territory or security. It also exposed the difference between diplomatic expectations and developments on the ground.

Panchsheel and the Bandung Principles

The Bandung Conference of 1955 adopted a broader set of 10 principles for international relations. These included respect for sovereignty, non-interference, peaceful settlement of disputes and respect for the United Nations Charter.

The Bandung Principles shared several ideas with Panchsheel, but the 2 sets should not be treated as identical.

Panchsheel contains 5 principles associated with the 1954 India-China agreement. The Bandung Conference of 1955 adopted 10 principles. Neither should be confused with the establishment of the Non-Aligned Movement in 1961.

Prelims focus

  • Panchsheel means Five Principles of Peaceful Coexistence.
  • Its formal expression appeared in the India-China agreement of 29 April 1954.
  • Jawaharlal Nehru and Zhou Enlai promoted Panchsheel internationally.
  • Non-aggression and non-interference are separate principles.
  • The Bandung Conference in 1955 adopted 10 principles.
  • Trap: Panchsheel is not a military alliance or a collective-defence agreement.

[Sources: Ministry of External Affairs, Panchsheel, External Publicity Division, June 2004, opening section and discussion of the 29 April and 28 June 1954 declarations; NCERT, Politics in India since Independence, Class 12, chapter 4, printed pp. 68-69; Non-Aligned Movement, Bandung Principles, official Uganda Chairmanship website, consulted 22 November 2026.]

pictures.caption: The 5 principles combine respect for sovereignty, restraint from aggression and mutually beneficial cooperation.

title: Panchsheel: The Five Principles of Peaceful Coexistence
